# 16-pairio — sources

Back-test entry `16-pairio.yaml`: Pairio, a voice assistant that helps factory technicians fix broken machines (YC
Spring 2026, P26). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only, read that day. Quotes are verbatim from the page named
(the launch-era site is in German; its quotes are given in German, with the author's English in brackets). "Author's
choice" marks the smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent. The launch era is the Launch YC
post of 2026-04-21 and the weeks around it (the founder's gap-11 rule: every figure pinned to the launch era where one
exists; anything later is marked as later).

Main sources (short names used below):
- [LYC] Launch YC: "Pairio – Fix broken equipment in factories faster", 2026-04-21 (created_at in the page data) — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Q18-pairio-fix-broken-equipment-in-factories-faster
- [WB] pairio.com as archived 2026-04-18, three days before launch (German) — https://web.archive.org/web/20260418031841/https://pairio.com/
- [YCP] YC company page, read 2026-10-22 — https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/pairio
- [BLOG] Pairio blog, "the same problems at every plant" (a founder's six weeks of US plant visits), datePublished 2026-05-17 — https://pairio.com/blog/same-problems-every-plant-every-industry/
- [FAQ] pairio.com FAQ, read 2026-10-22 — https://pairio.com/faq/
- [REF] pairio.com customer reference (Knipping), read 2026-10-22; figures "supplied by Knipping" — https://pairio.com/customer-references/
- [SITE] pairio.com, read 2026-10-22 — https://pairio.com
- [BLS] BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook, industrial machinery mechanics, machinery maintenance workers and millwrights, read 2026-10-22 — https://www.bls.gov/ooh/installation-maintenance-and-repair/industrial-machinery-mechanics-and-maintenance-workers-and-millwrights.htm

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Maintenance technicians and operators who fix machines on the production line.
   [LYC] "Pairio helps technicians and operators resolve faults faster with voice AI." [YCP] "AI mobile app that helps
   factory technicians fix broken machines". → `roles[technician]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`. Author's choice: the
   technician only (operators are named too, but the fix and the report are the technician's).

2. **What (the job).** Get the machine running again fast, and keep the fix for the next person.
   [LYC] "Unplanned equipment downtime costs global industries over $1.4 trillion every year – and the root cause isn't
   broken machines. It's broken knowledge transfer." [LYC] "With the average technician in the US now 50 years old,
   knowledge is literally walking out the door". → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** At the machine, when it fails, and afterwards when the fix should be written down.
   [LYC] "When a machine fails, resolution speed depends almost entirely on whether the one guy who's seen this before is
   working that day"; "Valuable technical clues are buried somewhere across 400 pages of OEM manuals or locked in outdated
   software"; "After spending 6 hours getting the line back up, the last thing a technician does is sit down and write a
   detailed fault report to institutionalize their knowledge". [FAQ] "Fundamentals and practical ways to use Pairio in
   day-to-day maintenance work." → `context.circumstance`, `occasion: machine breakdown`. Author's choice: the window
   {5, WORKING_DAYS} (a working-day rhythm) and Frequency 2 to 4 working days out of 5 -- daily for the team, not for
   each technician (header); Prevalence `p_80_100`.

4. **Which people.** Technicians at US plants that keep their own maintenance team.
   [LYC] "Ask: Can you introduce us to plant and maintenance managers at US manufacturing firms?" [WB] "Pairio richtet sich
   an Unternehmen mit eigener Instandhaltung - vom Mittelstand bis zum Konzern." [Pairio is for companies with their own
   maintenance, from mid-sized firms to groups.] → `context.segment`, `market: US`; the German plants are in the header.

5. **Who pays.** The plant; the maintenance manager chooses, the plant manager agrees.
   [LYC] "If you know anyone in plant operations or maintenance in US manufacturing we'd love to talk with them". [WB]
   quotes a "Meister & Abteilungsleiter Instandhaltung" [foreman and head of maintenance] as a user. → `persona.
   decision_maker: {role: manager}`; Buyer and payer tests "The plant manager" (listed with "The IT department"):
   author's choice, no source names who signs. Purchase friction's tested item, "Connecting it to SAP or Maximo": [FAQ]
   "including systems such as SAP, IFS, IBM Maximo, Oracle EAM Cloud, Hexagon, SharePoint, Outlook, and Asset API"; [WB]
   "Die genaue Anbindung hängt von Ihrer IT-Landschaft ab." [The exact connection depends on your IT landscape.] The IT
   security review and the plant-wide rollout sign-off are the author's. Commitment's step, "run a pilot on one
   production line": [REF] "A clearly scoped pilot creates evidence"; "Following a two-month pilot, the solution was
   integrated in four weeks." (later than launch; the launch-era site offers "Kostenlose Demo" [free demo]).

6. **Mechanism.** Ask by voice or photo; answers from the manuals and past repairs; speak the fix, get a report.
   [LYC] "Simply ask and instantly receive any available technical clue"; "Speak and let Pairio structure their learnings
   into reusable know-how"; "Use photos and videos to capture even more contextual knowledge". [WB] "Sprache, Foto oder
   Video rein - fertiger Bericht raus" [voice, photo or video in, finished report out]; "Pairio erkennt Fehlerbild,
   Maßnahmen, Ersatzteile und erstellt einen strukturierten Bericht." [Pairio recognises the fault, the actions, the spare
   parts and writes a structured report.] [YCP] "Users just take a picture of the broken machine and we search thousands
   of pages of manuals to find the right solution." → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`; Compatibility (a phone
   allowed at the machine — tested; manuals as files; quiet enough to speak) and Adoption friction (speak the fix when
   done — tested; photograph the fault first) are the author's, from the mechanism's own needs and [BLOG] ("tools that fit
   how technicians actually work, on mobile, in loud environments"). Relative advantage: shorter_time from [WB] "-25%
   MTTR", less_help_needed from [LYC]'s "the one guy who's seen this before"; the wording is the author's.

7. **Price and cost.** No price public; the cost is technician time.
   [WB] "Kostenlose Demo" and "Demo buchen" [free demo; book a demo], no price; [SITE] "Book a free demo", no price.
   → `commercial.price` AMOUNT_PERIOD $600 to $1,200 per technician a year is **the operator's reading** (about $50 to
   $100 a seat a month; header). Existing sacrifice, HOURS 150 to 300 of the breakdowns per technician a year: author's
   arithmetic -- 3 to 6 hours a week of a technician's time lost to hunting through manuals, waiting for the one person
   who knows, extra trips for tools and parts, and the report written afterwards, over about 50 working weeks; the scale
   is set by [LYC]'s "6 hours getting the line back up" and by [WB]'s "-25% MTTR" and "-80% Ablageaufwand" (the shares
   the company says it removes). The rate, $31 an hour, is [BLS] "$30.82 per hour" (May 2025 median), the author's
   stand-in. Ability to pay is read `budget` by the engine (hours never compare with dollars).

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from these public accounts; no respondent is a real person.
   [BLOG] "At a specialty manufacturer in Illinois, the maintenance team told me some shifts run with a single
   technician."; "The troubleshooting descriptions? Consistently useless. 'Reset machine.' 'Machine broken, fixed it.'
   'Called supplier.'"; "The work order says there's a problem with the injection molding machine. That's it. They show
   up, assess, go back for parts, come back again."; "When a conveyor goes down, every minute counts in a way that's
   directly visible to the customer."; "she'd watched a technician try to use ChatGPT out of desperation to solve a
   machine-specific problem."

The price split (5 of 7 at or above the reading) is the author's: no public figure says what share would pay. No
respondent carries the name of a customer, technician or founder in the sources.

## Status today

Same idea. [SITE] (English, 2026-10-22) describes the same assistant (fault reports, manual search, data analysis, work
instructions) now aimed at US plants, with the Knipping reference: [REF] "Knipping reduced mean time to repair (MTTR) by
25%, generated €500K in savings through avoided downtime, and achieved a 95% adoption rate." and "Four German locations
are already onboarded." [FAQ] "In suitable use cases, MTTR can be reduced by up to 25%, filing effort by up to 80%, and
onboarding time by up to 90%." Price today: still not public ("Book a free demo").

## Could not be sourced

- **Any price.** Nothing public at launch or today; the founder's price is the operator's reading (header, item 7), so the
  Price line measures that reading, not the company's price.
- **A per-plant money cost.** Only the global $1.4 trillion is public; the chain cost is the technicians' time instead
  (header).
- **The hours per technician a year.** The sources give one example (6 hours on one breakdown) and shares removed; the
  150 to 300 is the author's arithmetic.
- **A technician's hour.** [BLS]'s median stands in.
- **Who signs, and the purchase steps.** No source names the buyer above the maintenance manager; the plant manager, the
  IT department, the security review and the rollout sign-off are the author's (the SAP or Maximo connection is sourced).
- **How often one technician meets a breakdown.** "Day-to-day" is the team's rhythm; the 2 to 4 working days out of 5 is
  the author's.
- **First-person technician accounts.** No Launch HN or forum thread; the occasions are scripted from [BLOG] (the
  founder's own account of US visits) and [WB]'s two user quotes ("Mit der App kann ich alles direkt dokumentieren und
  muss mir keine Sorgen machen, dass ich etwas vergesse." [With the app I can document everything straight away and
  needn't worry about forgetting something.]).

insights.line: What would make it worth more?

whys.g1: The two answers say different things — one would pay more for proof of a downtime drop on one line, the other wouldn't pay for any app because the downtime comes from old machines and missing parts — so as a maintenance manager I'd leave each on its own too, and there's no existing group either one should have gone into.
whys.g2: There's no junk, explicit or off-topic answer on this line; both answers speak directly to what would make the tool worth more money.

founder.order_why: It runs from where the idea applies, to the problem, to the idea, then to who buys and pays and how the purchase happens, and ends with the setup before sending, which is how I'd explain Pairio to a plant myself.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 20 and 22 overlap: my first real step is already a pilot on one production line, so 'Offer a pilot?' asks it again. Screens 3 and 4 also carry the identical kicker and question, so they read as one screen shown twice.
founder.missing: Nothing asked whether a technician can actually use a phone and speak at the machine (phones allowed on the floor, noise, gloves). Whether it fits on the floor is the condition the whole voice-and-photo idea rests on, beyond the SAP or Maximo connection.

COMMERCIAL_B2B.order_why: The 'One more thing' screen about what would take the time in buying lands between 5 of 6 and 6 of 6, interrupting the numbered sequence right before the pilot question, when it reads like it belongs at the end.
COMMERCIAL_B2B.asked_twice: Screens 7 and 8 overlap: 7 asks how long the SAP/Maximo hookup would take, and 8 asks again what would take the time in buying, which for me is mostly that same integration and the plant manager sign-off already covered on screen 6.
COMMERCIAL_B2B.missing: Nothing asked whether it helps my less experienced techs fix machines they don't know (the Tech 1 to Tech 3 skill gap, which is my main reason to buy), or what a breakdown hour costs us in lost production, which is how I'd actually justify the price.

screens.why2: "Something that passes on how faults were fixed" needs a second read; I'd say "a voice assistant that helps techs fix machines and writes the fault report", and the six shapes take a moment to map to per-seat pricing.
screens.why3: My price is mine to say, even if it's still a reading and not public.
screens.why4: "A percent of the breakdowns" makes no sense as a price for a tool like this, and there is no plain per-seat or per-month option, though "a fixed fee each year" with the locked per technician · a year covers my answer.
screens.why5: The belief line keeps my $600 to $1,200 per technician a year, but the product drifted to only passing on past fixes and lost the voice/photo help at the machine and the manual search.
screens.instead: What price do you have in mind for a voice assistant that helps technicians fix machines and writes the fault report? — A fee per technician each year / A fee per technician each month / One fee per plant each year / A share of the downtime saved / One price, then nothing more / Free to them; chip: No price yet

screens.why1: Right after the price, asking who else has to sign off besides the maintenance manager is the obvious next step in how a plant buys.
screens.why2: Plain to me: 'maintenance manager', 'agree', 'buy' are exactly how I talk about selling into a plant, and the hint that 'Nobody' is an answer removes doubt.
screens.why3: Who else signs is something I know from my own demos and pilots: the plant manager on budget and IT on the SAP or Maximo connection.
screens.why4: A free box up to 25 words with 'Nobody' allowed fits this question, and 'Leave this out of the study' is a sensible escape.
screens.why5: I typed the plant manager and the IT department, but Keel's belief keeps only the plant manager, so the IT sign-off on the SAP or Maximo link is lost.
screens.instead: Same question; belief: The maintenance manager decides, and the plant manager and the IT department have to agree.

screens.why1: Right after I named who else has to agree, it makes sense for Keel to show me the full cast back before it builds Part 3 on it.
screens.why2: Maintenance technician, maintenance manager, plant manager and IT department are exactly the words we use about a US plant, and the instruction to reword or remove is clear on first read.
screens.why3: Who has the breakdown, who picks the tool and who signs off are things I know from every plant conversation.
screens.why4: The first two rows carry a role ('has the problem', 'decides to buy') but the plant manager and IT department rows carry none, so I can't tell whether Keel has them as 'has to agree' or something else, and the capitalisation is uneven ('maintenance technician' vs 'Maintenance manager', 'The plant manager').
screens.why5: The rows keep all four roles I typed, but the belief line names only the plant manager as having to agree and silently drops the IT department I listed alongside him for the SAP/Maximo connection and security review.
screens.instead: The people involved: maintenance technician · has the problem; maintenance manager · decides to buy; plant manager · has to agree; IT department · has to agree -- belief: The maintenance manager decides, and the plant manager and the IT department have to agree.

screens.why1: Right after I named the plant manager and IT as the ones who must agree, it makes sense to pick which one to test, and the plant manager is the one I'd bet on.
screens.why2: The choice itself is plain, but the bar's "something that passes on how faults were fixed" isn't how I or a maintenance manager would describe maintenance software, and "nothing is reworded here" takes a second read.
screens.why3: Who has to sign off when my buyer brings in new maintenance software is exactly what I'm trying to learn from US plant and maintenance managers.
screens.why4: The plant manager, the IT department and nobody else cover what I typed, and they are distinct and in my words.
screens.why5: The belief, that the maintenance manager decides and the plant manager agrees, is mine, but the bar shrinks Pairio to "something that passes on how faults were fixed" when it's a voice assistant that fixes and records.
screens.instead: Which one do you want to test? The plant manager / The IT department / Nobody else, with the bar: holds if at least 2 in 3 maintenance managers say the plant manager had to agree the last time they bought new maintenance software.

screens.why1: Right after I named what could slow a purchase, Keel shows the list back for me to check before it tests the belief, which is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: SAP, Maximo, IT security review, plant-wide rollout and budget approval are everyday words to me and to the maintenance managers I sell to.
screens.why3: Integration with the plant's CMMS or ERP, security review and rollout sign-off are exactly the hurdles I hit in every plant conversation, and Knipping went through them.
screens.why4: Each row is a real hurdle, but 'Sign-off for a plant-wide rollout' and 'Budget approval' are often the same plant manager signature, and 'SAP or Maximo' leaves out IFS, Oracle EAM and other CMMS we connect to.
screens.why5: The tested item is my SAP or Maximo connection, and the belief of about 6 weeks or not needed fits our own record of a four-week integration after the pilot.
screens.instead: Rows: Connecting it to the CMMS (SAP, Maximo); An IT security review; A pilot on one line first; Plant manager sign-off and budget

screens.why1: Right after I listed what could slow a purchase, it is obvious that I now pick the one step to test and say how long I expect it to take, which is the question every plant deal turns on for us.
screens.why2: The screen is mostly plain, but 'how long would this step take before it went through' fits a sign-off better than a connection to SAP or Maximo, which gets done or goes live rather than goes through, and the same hint is printed twice, so I read it twice.
screens.why3: I know from the demos and the Knipping rollout roughly how long an SAP or Maximo hookup takes, and a maintenance manager knows how long their own IT takes to connect a new tool to the CMMS.
screens.why4: The four steps are the real hurdles in a plant purchase, in the words a plant uses, with no overlap; SAP or Maximo stands fairly for the CMMS list, and days, weeks and months cover the answer.
screens.why5: The belief keeps what I picked and typed, connecting it to SAP or Maximo within about 6 weeks, and 'or not need it' fairly covers plants that run Pairio without any connection, so nothing drifts or leaks.
screens.instead: Which one do you want to test? (same four steps) -- If they bought it, how long until this step is done: connecting it to SAP or Maximo would take about [6] [weeks].

screens.why1: After who signs and what slows a purchase, asking for the first committed step a plant would take is the natural close of the selling questions.
screens.why2: 'First real step' with the hint naming time, data, money or a signature is plain to me as a founder selling into maintenance departments.
screens.why3: I know what I ask plants for, a scoped pilot on one line, so I can answer this straight from my own sales conversations.
screens.why4: It is a free-text box with a single escape chip, 'Leave this out of the study', which fits a founder who has no commitment step to test.
screens.why5: Keel's belief keeps my pilot on one production line, but it adds 'now' and 'In most cases', which turn my step into a claim about how soon and how many that I never typed.
screens.instead: Belief: 'The maintenance manager would agree to run a pilot on one production line.' Drop the 'now' and the 'in most cases'.

screens.why1: Right after I named the first real step, this screen plays it back as the belief and bar Keel will test, which is the obvious last piece of the commercial chain.
screens.why2: 'Run a pilot on one production line' is how I and the maintenance managers I talk to describe a first step, so I understand it on first reading.
screens.why3: Whether to start a line pilot is a call I know maintenance managers make themselves, and it is the step I am asking them for in every demo.
screens.why4: The screen shows my step and the bar to read and save, with no options or chips of its own to judge.
screens.why5: It keeps my step word for word; Keel only adds 'now', which is a fair reading of a first step even if a manager might put it after budget season.

screens.why1: Right after I named the first step (a pilot on one production line), asking whether to collect pilot sign-ups is the obvious next thing before the study goes out, and US plant contacts are exactly what I'm after.
screens.why2: "Offer a pilot?" with a yes/no and a hint that says what the respondent sees and where I find the yeses is plain on first read.
screens.why3: Whether I want to ask strangers for a pilot is my own decision, and I can answer it at once.
screens.why4: Yes or no is complete and distinct for this choice, and no escape is needed.
screens.why5: The line respondents get is the generic "Would you try this for real?" rather than my step, a pilot on one production line, which a technician can't agree to alone, so the ask drifts a little from what I typed.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? Respondents get: "Would your plant try this on one production line? Leave your email." — Yes, ask them / No pilot

screens.why_b1: The verdict line says 'Did not hold' and gives the deciding number beside it: 3 of 7 managers expect the SAP or Maximo connection to take longer than 6 weeks.
screens.why_b2: Every card gives its count and bar, but Existing sacrifice counts 4 of 6 when 7 answered, and nothing on the page says why one person dropped out, so I had to look twice.
screens.why_b3: Five beliefs are my words, but Existing sacrifice now says maintenance managers 'spend' 150 to 300 hours per technician, when I meant the technicians lose that time to breakdowns; it is still recognisable.
screens.why_b4: Nothing says what the integration result means for me, such as running the pilot without SAP or Maximo first or planning for 6 weeks to 3 months; the statement only explains who answered.
screens.why_b5: The n is visible on every card, the cards that only reach their bar are marked 'at the bar' rather than called strong, Ability to pay is left uncalled at 4 answered, and the page explains that the stage verdict is the worst card.
screens.instead: Did not hold on one card: 3 of 7 managers expect the SAP or Maximo connection to take 6 weeks to 3 months, so offer a pilot that runs before integration and plan the connection afterwards; three other cards pass only at their bar, so treat them as thin.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "4 of 6 spend 150 hours or more per technician a year · bar 4 of 6 · at the bar", so I see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: The axis is hours per technician a year from 0 to 400, the median of 190 is marked, and the strip shows 4 for and 2 against with the marker at 4 of 6, so what is counted, over how many people and where the bar sits are all plain at once.
screens.why_b3: This is my 150-to-300-hours figure, but it was not among the beliefs I checked on the way in, and "maintenance managers already spend" reads oddly, because the hours are my technicians' time at the machine, not the managers' own.
screens.why_b4: The So line says the cost is real for 4 of 6 and points me to the Price card to see whether they would pay to remove it, which is exactly the next question for my pitch.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible (7 answered, 6 counted, Sabine's "none" counted as 0, Arturo not counted), and "a small group: a lean, not a call" keeps a result sitting exactly on the bar from being oversold.
screens.instead: Holding up, but only just: 4 of 6 is exactly the bar, and one more manager below 150 hours would tip it; the 150 to 300 hours are your technicians' time on breakdowns.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "5 of 7 at $600 or more · bar 5 of 7 · at the bar", so I see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: The bins, the for/against labels on each, the 7 people and the marker at 5 of 7 (at least 2 in 3) all read on first look.
screens.why_b3: Price is plainly my product's price question, but I never set or checked $600 to $1,200, since no price of ours is public, yet the card tells me "You said" it.
screens.why_b4: The So line only restates 5 of 7 and points me to Ability to pay; it never says that four of the five sit under $1,000, which is what I'd act on when I quote a price.
screens.why_b5: It is honest about n ("a small group: a lean, not a call") and the hold is exactly at the bar, but calling the whole $600 to $1,200 range "holding up" softly overstates the top end, which only one manager reached.
screens.instead: Just at the bar: 5 of 7 would pay $600 or more, but 4 of them under $1,000, so quote the low end of this range (Keel's reading, not your price) and test $1,200 on a pilot line.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits beside '4 answered · 5 needed', but the count line below says '5 answered · 4 counted', so I can't tell whether it's four or five, or what the five refers to.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts where the money would come from, over the 4 counted managers, with 3 for, 1 against, 1 grey cell, and the marker at 3 of 4 (at least 2 in 3), all plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: I never checked an Ability to pay line on the way in; this one is Keel's, built from my $600 to $1,200 reading, and I recognise it but it isn't my words.
screens.why_b4: The So line says Price decides this stage, but the stage page says Purchase friction did and my Price card held at the bar; it also says this waits until 5 name my price, when Gloria, Richard, Darnell, Priya and Arturo already did.
screens.why_b5: It says 'a lean, not a call' and keeps n visible, but 'only 5 of 7 would pay' casts a held Price line as a shortfall, and the 4-versus-5 answered mismatch muddies the count.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 3 of the 4 managers who named a source would pay from a budget line they already have (bar 2 in 3), and Arturo couldn't say; one more clear answer decides it, so ask Arturo where the money would come from after his demo.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "6 of 7 as you said or easier · bar 5 of 7", so I see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts who must agree to a $600-per-technician deal across 7 managers, with the bar marked at 5 of 7, and the strip's 6 for against 1 makes it plain at first look.
screens.why_b3: The title and belief line are the ones I checked word for word: the maintenance manager decides, and the plant manager has to agree.
screens.why_b4: "Plan for the plant manager in most deals" tells me concretely to build the plant manager into my sales motion, and that one in seven may close without that step.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible and the count line says outright "a small group: a lean, not a call", so 6 of 7 is not oversold.
screens.instead: Plan for the plant manager in most deals; 1 of 7 could sign alone, and at a multi-plant group corporate engineering may own the choice, so ask who picks the software before you pitch.

screens.why_b1: The status 'Did not hold' sits right beside '3 of 7 expect longer than 6 weeks · bar: no more than 2 of 7', so I see both the verdict and the one vote that decided it.
screens.why_b2: The bands and their counts read at once, but the bar is given as 'no more than 2 of 7' against in the header and as 'your bar · 5 of 7' for on the chart and strip, so I need a second look to see these are the same line.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Purchase friction and the belief line is word for word the one I checked, SAP or Maximo within about 6 weeks or not needed, though the bar line 'You said connecting it to SAP or Maximo.' is a stray fragment.
screens.why_b4: It tells me to plan for an integration cycle of 6 weeks to 3 months and points me to Insights for what would take the time, which is a concrete change to how I would sell into a plant.
screens.why_b5: The card does say 'a small group: a lean, not a call', but it calls 6 weeks to 3 months 'most often' when 2 to under 6 weeks also has 3, and it tells me to plan for the longer cycle even though 4 of 7 said faster.
screens.instead: Did not hold, by one vote: 3 of 7 managers expect SAP or Maximo to take 6 weeks to 3 months, as many as expect 2 to 6 weeks. With only 7 answers, plan for up to 3 months with plants like Gloria's, Mei-Ling's and Darnell's, and see on Insights what slows them.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside its deciding number, 5 of 7 said yes against a bar of 5 of 7, and the screen says it is at the bar.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts maintenance managers' answers to the pilot question over all 7, with 5 for and 2 against, and the strip's marker sits at 5, so what is counted, over whom and where the bar falls are all plain at once.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Commitment and carries my belief word for word: in most cases the maintenance manager would run a pilot on one production line now.
screens.why_b4: 'Book them into it' is a concrete next step: turn the five who said yes into actual one-line pilots.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible and the count line says this is a small group, 'a lean, not a call', so nothing is claimed beyond the seven who answered.
screens.instead: 5 of 7 would run a pilot on one line, exactly at your bar, so one more 'no' would flip it; book those five into pilots now and treat a signed pilot, not a 'yes', as the proof.

screens.why_b1: Each box opens on its verdict (Did not hold / Holding up) with the deciding count beside it: 3 of 7 against a bar of no more than 2 of 7, 5 of 7 at the bar, 6 of 7 against a bar of 5 of 7.
screens.why_b3: Purchase friction, Price and Buyer and payer carry the belief lines I checked on the way in, word for word: SAP or Maximo within about 6 weeks, $600 to $1,200 per technician a year, the maintenance manager decides and the plant manager agrees.
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what to do. The one line that failed, Purchase friction, has no reason at all (0 asked their why, 3 never saw it), so I can't tell whether the delay is the SAP/Maximo hookup, IT security or the rollout sign-off, which is exactly what I'd need to change the pitch or the integration.
screens.why_b5: The counts and the 'at the bar' marks stay visible and nothing is called strong, but 'the 2 who said no' on Price lumps Mei-Ling, who would pay $250 to under $600, in with Sabine, who would pay nothing.
screens.why_b6: Mei-Ling's 'show me the downtime drop on one line' and Darnell's corporate engineering choosing for every plant add a little beyond my picks, but the failed line, where I most needed to learn something, is empty.
screens.instead: Under Purchase friction, ask the 3 who expect longer than 6 weeks what would take the time (the SAP/Maximo connection, the IT security review or the rollout sign-off), and on Price say '1 would pay less, 1 would not pay' instead of '2 said no'.

screens.why1: As the opening screener it is obvious why they ask: they want plants where the maintenance crew is our own people, not a contractor, and mine is.
screens.why2: I get it straight away, but nobody says 'your US plant' when every plant I run is in the US, and a plant has one maintenance team or crew, not 'teams'.
screens.why3: Whether we keep maintenance in-house or contract it out is my call and my budget, so I can answer without guessing.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it for a gate, and no escape chip is right here; a plant that's mostly in-house with a few contractors would still say Yes.
screens.why5: It reads like the founder's segment line ('US plants that run their own maintenance teams') pasted in, not put in a plant manager's words about their own shop, so it has drifted a little toward the brief's wording.
screens.why6: It is short and one question, but the spoken form drops the 'Yes or no.' the screener is supposed to end on, and 'your US plant' sounds stilted when heard.
screens.instead: Does your plant have its own maintenance crew on staff, rather than contracting it out? Yes; No

screens.why1: Right after the screener confirms we run our own maintenance team, showing me the idea before the buying questions is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: SAP, Maximo, wiring diagrams and fault reports are everyday words to me, but 'a sourced answer and report' doesn't tell me what the thing is; I'd call it a phone assistant for my techs.
screens.why3: My techs chasing manuals at a down machine and then skipping the write-up is exactly my week, so I can judge this from what I see on my floor.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options.
screens.why5: The product reveal is meant to be here, but the opening line is the founder's label rather than saying what it is, and 'They speak, or take photos or video of the fix' reads like notes, not how I'd describe it.
screens.why6: It can be said, but it runs long: the colon lists, 'SAP, Maximo or SharePoint' in one breath, and a belief line that repeats the how instead of pointing back to it make it a lot to hold in one hearing.
screens.instead: Imagine Pairio, a phone assistant for your maintenance techs. At the machine, a tech asks by voice or photo and gets an answer from your manuals, wiring diagrams and past repairs, with where it came from. Afterwards they talk through the fix or snap photos, and it writes the work order into your CMMS, such as SAP or Maximo. The people building it believe this gets machines back up faster and leaves a real record of every fix.

screens.why1: Asking what breakdowns cost my team makes sense right after the idea card, but 'the breakdowns' points back at something nobody named, so it lands abruptly.
screens.why2: I'd have to read it twice to work out which breakdowns are meant, and 'hours per technician' over a year makes me do averaging in my head before I can answer.
screens.why3: I know roughly how much downtime work my guys do, but a per-tech yearly hour figure is something I'd have to pull from the CMMS or just guess.
screens.why4: A number box is right, but having both 'None' and 'I can't recall' as chips gives two escapes, and 'None' just duplicates typing 0.
screens.why5: Nothing leaks, but the founder's window is the last five working days and this stretches it to a whole year, which drifts from what was meant.
screens.why6: The question says fine, but the instruction tail 'or a low and a high; none is 0' is clunky to hear and adds a second set of directions after the question.
screens.instead: In the last five working days, about how many hours did your team spend getting broken-down machines running again? (number of hours; escape: I can't recall)

screens.why1: Right after I told them how many hours my techs lose to breakdowns, asking what the tool is worth per tech a year is the natural next question for the one who signs for it.
screens.why2: Worth to me a year, per technician, in dollars is how I already budget tools for my crew, so I can answer it on first read.
screens.why3: I price tools per tech all the time, but 'a sourced answer and report' doesn't tell me what it does on a down machine, so my number would be partly a guess.
screens.why4: The bands run cleanly from under $250 to $2,500 or more with no overlap, 'I wouldn't pay for this' is there, and 'I can't say' fits as the escape.
screens.why5: 'A sourced answer and report' sounds like somebody's pitch words, not mine, and it drifts from fixing a down machine fast and logging the fix.
screens.why6: Three bands and a 'wouldn't pay' are easy to hold, but 'Or say you can't say' trips the ear, and 'Pairio' with a year and a per-technician tacked on is a bit of a mouthful.
screens.instead: Imagine Pairio, which tells your tech how to fix the down machine and writes up the repair record. What would it be worth to you a year, per technician? Under $250 · $250 to under $600 · $600 to under $1,000 · $1,000 to under $2,500 · $2,500 or more · I wouldn't pay for this · escape: I can't say

screens.why1: Right after I put a price on it, asking where that money would actually come from is the obvious next question for someone who holds the maintenance budget.
screens.why2: On screen it says "$600 to $1,000 a year" but I gave that per technician, so I'd stop and wonder whether it means per tech or for the whole crew. Options like "there was no budget" and "someone signed off" also read in the past tense under a question about what would happen.
screens.why3: I run the maintenance budget and I know exactly whether something like this comes out of my existing spend, needs the plant manager's sign-off, or gets taken from parts or contractors.
screens.why4: The four cover it, but they're in the past tense under an if-question, and "There was no budget for it" isn't really a source of money; it reads more like "I couldn't fund it," so it needs rewording rather than being wrong.
screens.why5: It points back to my own price and asks about funding; nothing of the founder's product or plan leaks beyond the idea I was already shown.
screens.why6: It's short, one question, and four options I can hold, but "Or say you can't say" trips the ear, and the past-tense options sound off after "if you went ahead."
screens.instead: You said about $600 to $1,000 a year per technician. If you went ahead at that, where would the money come from? Our maintenance budget as it stands · A new line the plant manager signs off · Moved from other maintenance spending · We couldn't find the money · I can't say

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I could sign off on the money, asking what would hold up the rollout is the natural next thing.
screens.why2: SAP and Maximo are plain to me, but 'before it went through' fits a purchase order, not an integration job, so I had to read it twice.
screens.why3: I'd have a rough idea, but hooking anything into SAP is IT's project and their queue, so I'd be guessing at their timeline.
screens.why4: The bands are clean, but a plant on Fiix, UpKeep, eMaint or paper has no true answer, and 'It wouldn't be needed' blurs 'no hookup needed' with 'we don't run either one'.
screens.why5: The step reads as the founder's, but 'went through' turns a technical hookup into an approval, which drifts a little.
screens.why6: Said aloud it is one question, four short options I can hold, one escape, and a two-choice follow-up, so it says well.
screens.instead: If you bought Pairio, how long would it take to hook it up to your CMMS, like SAP or Maximo? Under 2 weeks · 2 to under 6 weeks · 6 weeks to 3 months · 3 to 6 months · Over 6 months · We wouldn't need to hook it up

screens.why1: It comes straight after I said hooking it into SAP or Maximo would take a while, so asking what eats that time is the obvious next thing.
screens.why2: The words are plain, but the last screen was about connecting it to SAP or Maximo and this one says buying, so I'd stop and wonder whether you mean the IT hookup or the purchase order and approvals.
screens.why3: I know exactly what holds these things up at my plant: IT's queue, getting a Maximo interface built, corporate security review, and getting the plant manager to sign.
screens.why4: It's a box to type in, with no options to judge.
screens.why5: The step it should follow up on was connecting it to SAP or Maximo, and widening that to buying Pairio drifts from it a little, though nothing new about the product leaks to me.
screens.why6: One short question said in one breath, easy to answer out loud.
screens.instead: What would take the time in connecting Pairio to SAP or Maximo?

screens.why1: After the price, who pays, who signs off and how long buying it would take, asking whether I'd actually try it is the natural last question.
screens.why2: Running a pilot on one line is exactly how I'd put trying a new tool with my techs, and I get it on first read.
screens.why3: Deciding whether we trial a tool on a line is my call as maintenance manager, so I can answer it straight.
screens.why4: The scale is lopsided: there is a firm yes, then a probably not and a no, but no probably yes, so a leaning-yes answer like mine has nowhere honest to go.
screens.why5: The question itself is clean, but the card above it, 'a sourced answer and report', reads like someone's internal label rather than anything a maintenance person would call a tool.
screens.why6: Heard once it is short, a single question, and three options I can hold, ending on a plain no.
screens.instead: If it were ready today, would you run a pilot on one production line, or not? Yes, I'd run a pilot · Probably yes · Probably not · No
